302.title: The turning
302.hook: the Mevlevi order's turning ceremony, one hand up, one hand down
302.howItsDone: Mevlevi Sufis perform the sama' ceremony with the ney and drum, turning with the right palm up and the left palm down; other Muslims, including some scholars, do not use music or dance in worship, and Muslims differ on it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, hal, a state of the heart: moods that come to teach and then leave, and days that take their turns. Your line: every state is a guest.

The picture travels far beyond Turkey, on posters, postcards and screens: men in tall honey-colored felt hats and long white skirts, turning, turning, skirts flaring out like bells, heads tilted, eyes half closed. People call them whirling dervishes. It looks like a dance. The people who do it call it something else, and their word is about the ears, not the feet.
screen: `TALL HATS, WHITE SKIRTS.` → `TURNING, EYES HALF CLOSED.` → `A WORD ABOUT THE EARS.`

segments.voice: The word is sama'. It means listening, from the same root as as-Sami', the All-Hearing, one of the names of God. For Sufis, sama' means listening to music, poetry or the Qur'an with the heart until you're moved by it. The Mevlevi order, named for Rumi, Mawlana, turned that listening into a ceremony. Tradition says Rumi himself would sometimes turn in ecstasy, and people tell a story that it began when he heard goldbeaters hammering in the Konya bazaar. The formal ceremony was shaped after his death, by his son and later generations. Everything in it carries meaning. The tall hat is said to stand for the tombstone of the ego. The white skirt, the shroud. The black cloak they take off at the start, the grave left behind. The music: the ney, the reed flute, and a drum. And the arms: right palm up to the sky, left palm down to the earth. As the Mevlevis explain it, what comes from God is received through the right hand and passed on to the world through the left. The turner keeps nothing. Receive, give. They turn around their own hearts, and they turn together, like planets. In modern Turkey the orders were closed, and for decades the ceremony survived mostly as a cultural performance. UNESCO now lists it as part of humanity's cultural heritage. And Muslims hold different views on music in worship: some scholars allow musical sama', and others do not accept it at all. Those differences come up again soon.
screen: `SAMA' — LISTENING.` · `HAT, SHROUD, CLOAK.` · `RIGHT HAND UP, LEFT HAND DOWN.` · `NOT ALL MUSLIMS ACCEPT IT.` · then, large: `RECEIVE, GIVE.`

segments.voice: If you can stand safely, lift your right hand a little, palm up, let your left hang low, palm down, soften your eyes, and turn slowly once, all the way round, feeling the floor under your feet; then stand still and breathe. If you can't stand, just turn your palms, one up, one down, and sit with them. Picture receiving through one and giving through the other.
Sama'. Listening with the heart; for the Mevlevis, the turning ceremony, one hand up, one hand down. Today's word.
Your line: receive, give. One palm to the sky, one to the earth. See you tomorrow.

303.title: The teacher and the chain
303.hook: Sufi orders pass teaching from master to student in chains
303.howItsDone: Members of Sufi orders take a pledge, bay'ah, with a living shaykh and learn the practices of their order's chain; some recite the names of their chain, while other Muslims learn the faith from scholars and teachers without joining an order.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the turning, sama': listening with the heart, right palm up, left palm down. Your line: receive, give.

A coach takes your wrist, moves it an inch, and suddenly the swing is right. No manual could have told you that inch. A carpenter's apprentice stands beside the bench for years before the cuts come clean. Some knowledge only travels hand to hand. Sufis say the inner path is like that. You can read about it, as al-Ghazali did, but to walk it, the classic Sufi handbooks say, you need a guide who walked it before you, who learned from someone before them, and so on, back and back.
screen: `A COACH MOVES YOUR WRIST AN INCH.` → `SOME THINGS TRAVEL HAND TO HAND.` → `A GUIDE WHO WALKED IT FIRST.`

segments.voice: The Arabic word is silsilah, a chain, like links of metal. In a Sufi order, every teacher, a shaykh, learned from a teacher, who learned from a teacher, all the way back, the Sufis say, to the Prophet ﷺ himself. Students often memorize the names in their chain, and some recite them. Sufi tradition traces chains through 'Ali, the Prophet's cousin and son-in-law, and the Naqshbandi order is known for its chain through Abu Bakr. Muslims already knew this shape from the hadith. Every hadith comes with an isnad, a chain of narrators: I heard it from so-and-so, who heard it from so-and-so, who heard the Prophet say. Hadith scholars examine each link. The Sufi chain works the same way, but it passes down more than words: a way of practice, and what Sufis call blessing. The link is made by a pledge, bay'ah, often with a handclasp between teacher and student. Sufis connect it to a verse in the Qur'an about the companions who pledged themselves to the Prophet. In Pickthall's words: "The Hand of Allah is above their hands." A chain of hands, one on another, back through the centuries, and above them all, in the Sufis' understanding, God's. There's a warning in the tradition too: a chain is only as good as its links, and Sufi writers themselves warn against false teachers. And a Muslim can learn the faith deeply without joining any order. But for those who take the pledge, their own name becomes the newest link.
screen: `SILSILAH — A CHAIN.` · `BACK TO THE PROPHET, THROUGH 'ALI OR ABU BAKR.` · `LIKE THE ISNAD OF A HADITH.` · `BAY'AH — THE PLEDGE AND THE HANDCLASP.` · then, large: `A CHAIN OF HANDS.`

segments.voice: Think of the people who taught you something that mattered: a parent, a teacher at school, an imam, a coach, a boss, an older friend, and go back one more link if you can: who taught them? Say their names quietly, one by one, like a chain. If you pray, you can pray for every name on your chain.
Silsilah. The chain of teachers in a Sufi order, reaching back, hand to hand, toward the Prophet. Today's word.
Your line: a chain of hands. Every teacher once learned from a teacher. Day three hundred three, done.

304.title: The orders
304.hook: Qadiri, Naqshbandi, Chishti, Shadhili, Mevlevi and more across the world
304.howItsDone: Sufi orders, turuq, gather members around a shaykh for teaching, remembrance and service; the Qadiri, Chishti, Naqshbandi, Shadhili, Tijani and others have followers from West Africa to Southeast Asia, and many Muslims belong to no order.

segments.voice: Yesterday, silsilah, the chain: teachers hand to hand, back through the centuries. Your line: a chain of hands. Today, where those chains lead.

A big city has one great mosque at its center, and people walk to it from every direction. Some come down the wide avenue. Some take the back alleys they grew up in. Some walk slowly, some fast, some sing on the way, some go in silence. They all end up at the same door. Over the centuries, the chains of Sufi teachers grew into communities with their own names, their own practices, their own personalities, spread from Morocco to Indonesia. Each one is called by a word that means a road.
screen: `ONE MOSQUE, MANY STREETS.` → `FROM MOROCCO TO INDONESIA.` → `EACH ONE CALLED A ROAD.`

segments.voice: The word is tariqah: a way, a road, a path. Sufis often put it like this: the shari'ah, the law, is the road everyone walks. The tariqah is the way of walking it, with a guide. And the haqiqah, the reality, is where the road leads. Now, five roads. The Qadiri order, named for 'Abd al-Qadir al-Jilani, a preacher and scholar in Baghdad, with circles from West Africa to South Asia. The Chishti order, rooted in India through Mu'in al-Din Chishti, buried in Ajmer, known for open kitchens that feed anyone, and for devotional music, qawwali. The Naqshbandi order, named for Baha' al-Din Naqshband of Bukhara, known for silent remembrance of God, and a phrase: solitude in the crowd, keeping the heart with God while you're busy in the market. The Shadhili order, from Abu al-Hasan al-Shadhili, in North Africa and Egypt, which teaches its members not to leave their jobs and families, but to find the path inside ordinary life. And the Mevlevi, Rumi's order, with the turning from two days ago. There are many more: the Tijani across West Africa, the Rifa'i, the Suhrawardi, the Ba 'Alawi of Yemen. They differ in style, loud or quiet, music or none, withdrawing or staying in the world. Each order would say its own road is a way of following the same Prophet to the same God. Many roads in.
screen: `SHARI'AH, TARIQAH, HAQIQAH.` · `QADIRI AND CHISHTI.` · `NAQSHBANDI AND SHADHILI.` · `LOUD OR QUIET, MUSIC OR NONE.` · then, large: `MANY ROADS IN.`

Say its name to yourself a few times, and picture its road. If you pray, you can pray for the people walking that road right now.
Tariqah. A road; a Sufi order, a way of walking the one path with a guide. Today's word.
Your line: many roads in. Loud or quiet, each one a way of walking. Day three hundred four.

305.title: Gathered remembrance
305.hook: circles of dhikr, sung or silent
305.howItsDone: Muslims remember God with short phrases after prayer and throughout the day, often counting on the fingers or prayer beads; in Sufi orders, members also gather in circles of dhikr, aloud or silent, while some scholars object to group dhikr in unison.

segments.voice: Yesterday, tariqah, the orders: Qadiri, Chishti, Naqshbandi, Shadhili, Mevlevi, many roads to one door. Your line: many roads in.

The same Thursday night, two rooms. In the first, in a city in Morocco or Egypt, people sit shoulder to shoulder in a circle. Someone begins a phrase and the whole room takes it up, rocking gently, the sound rising and falling like surf, for an hour. In the second, somewhere in Central Asia or Turkey, people sit in a circle too, heads bowed, eyes closed. Nobody makes a sound. The only sound is breathing. Ask either room what it's doing, and you'd get the same answer.
screen: `A ROOM THAT RISES LIKE SURF.` → `A ROOM IN TOTAL SILENCE.` → `BOTH DOING THE SAME THING.`

segments.voice: The thing is dhikr: remembrance of God, usually by repeating short phrases. La ilaha illa Allah, there is no god but God. Subhan Allah, glory be to God. Or simply Allah. You've met dhikr before on this path: a Muslim who says these after prayer is already doing it. What the orders added was the circle, the halqah, remembrance done together. Some circles say it aloud, sometimes with singing and a drum. That's jahri, out loud. Others, like the Naqshbandis, keep it silent, in the heart. That's khafi, hidden. Both point to the same verse, in Pickthall's words: "Verily in the remembrance of Allah do hearts find rest!" And to a hadith in Sahih Muslim: whenever people sit together remembering God, the angels surround them, mercy covers them, calm descends on them, and God mentions them to those who are with Him. In another, in al-Bukhari, God says, in a hadith qudsi: if my servant remembers Me in himself, I remember him in Myself; if he remembers Me in a gathering, I remember him in a gathering better than that. Muslims do differ here. Some scholars object to group dhikr in unison or with music, seeing it as later than the Prophet's practice; others defend it. More on that in two days. But the silent circle points at the heart of it all: the tongue can say the words, but the goal is that the heart says them. The heart says it.
screen: `DHIKR — REMEMBRANCE.` · `JAHRI ALOUD, KHAFI HIDDEN.` · `IN REMEMBRANCE HEARTS FIND REST.` · `ANGELS SURROUND THE CIRCLE.` · then, large: `THE HEART SAYS IT.`

segments.voice: Sit, eyes closed if you like, and let your breath settle into its own pace. If you pray, say a phrase silently with each breath, inside, not with your lips: Allah on the breath in, Allah on the breath out, or la ilaha illa Allah across one breath. If you don't pray, rest on the breath alone, counting it or simply following it, and let the heart do the saying.
Gathered remembrance. Circles of dhikr, sung aloud or held in silence, remembering God together. Today's word.
Your line: the heart says it. Even when the tongue is still. See you tomorrow.

306.title: The self to be trained
306.hook: the self that commands evil, that blames itself, that is at peace (12:53; 75:2; 89:27)
306.howItsDone: Muslims speak of struggling with the nafs as a lifelong part of faith, and Sufi teachers guide students through its stages, commanding, blaming and at peace, with remembrance, self-examination and service.

segments.voice: Yesterday, gathered remembrance: circles of dhikr, some rising like surf, some in total silence. Your line: the heart says it.

It's eleven at night. One voice in you says: one more episode, one more slice, send the angry text, you deserve it. Ten minutes later, another: why did you do that? You always do that. And once in a while, on a good day, there's a third thing, not really a voice at all. A quiet. You did the right thing, or you didn't and you've made it right, and you're simply at rest. Everyone knows those three. The Qur'an names them, in three different surahs, and Sufis built a whole map of the inner life on them.
screen: `ONE MORE, YOU DESERVE IT.` → `WHY DID YOU DO THAT?` → `A QUIET.`

segments.voice: The Arabic word is nafs: soul, self, or ego, depending on the sentence. The first nafs is in the story of Yusuf. In Pickthall's translation: "the (human) soul enjoineth unto evil," except where God has mercy. Commentators differ on who says those words, Yusuf or the wife of the man who bought him, but all agree on what they describe: the self that pushes, that grabs, that wants now. An-nafs al-ammarah, the self that commands. The second is in a short Meccan surah, where God swears an oath by it: "Nay, I swear by the accusing soul." An-nafs al-lawwamah, the self that blames: the voice at eleven-ten. God swears by it. The conscience that stings is honored, not despised. The third comes near the end of surah 89, addressed with great tenderness: "But ah! thou soul at peace!" An-nafs al-mutma'innah, the self at rest, invited to return to its Lord, content. Sufi teachers read the three as stages. The self isn't evil, and it isn't thrown away. It's trained, the way you'd train a strong young horse: not broken, but taught. The work of the path is moving from commanding, through blaming, toward peace. A hadith in al-Bukhari fits: the strong one isn't the one who wins the wrestling match, but the one who controls himself when angry. Train the self.

segments.voice: Replay your day so far and name each self that spoke: the commanding one, pushing for more, faster, now; the blaming one, stinging, maybe too harshly; and any moment of quiet, even a few seconds. Name them without judging them, and thank the blaming self for caring. If you pray, you can ask God to bring your self to peace.
Nafs. The self, in three stages in the Qur'an: commanding, blaming, and at peace. Today's word.
Your line: train the self. Not broken, but taught, like a strong young horse. Day three hundred six.

307.title: Where Muslims differ
307.hook: some embrace orders and saints' shrines, others hold these as later additions, and all say keep to the Qur'an
307.howItsDone: Muslims differ on Sufi orders, visiting saints' shrines and music in worship: some embrace them, Salafi Muslims and others reject them as later additions, and others take a middle position, while all appeal to the Qur'an and the sunnah.

segments.voice: Yesterday, nafs: the self that commands, the self that blames, the self at peace. Your line: train the self.

Friday, just after the prayer. A family drives out to a saint's tomb, a white dome with green cloth over the grave. They recite al-Fatiha for him, ask God for help near the resting place of a man they love, and give food to the poor at the gate. Their cousins, just as devout, would never go. They'd say, with conviction, that this isn't how the Prophet and his companions practiced, and that prayer should be directed to God alone, with nothing that looks like a go-between. Two weeks on the Sufi path, and now, honestly: where Muslims differ.
screen: `A WHITE DOME, A GREEN CLOTH.` → `COUSINS WHO WOULD NEVER GO.` → `BOTH DEVOUT.`

segments.voice: For many centuries, Sufism sat inside the mainstream of Muslim learning. Great scholars of law, like al-Ghazali, were Sufis. Across the Ottoman lands, South Asia, West Africa and Southeast Asia, the orders were part of ordinary life, and visiting the shrines of saints was common. In many places, it still is. Other Muslims have long criticized parts of it. The medieval scholar Ibn Taymiyyah respected early Sufis like Junayd, but condemned practices at graves that he believed compromised tawhid, the oneness of God. Modern Salafi movements, which aim to follow the salaf, the first generations of Muslims, hold that orders, shrine visits and musical sama' are later additions, bid'ah; some reject tasawwuf as a separate path altogether. Others stand in between: they value tasawwuf as purifying the heart, and question some practices. Shia Muslims visit the shrines of the Prophet's family, and their relation to the Sufi orders varies. These are real differences, sometimes painful ones. But every side argues from the Qur'an and the sunnah. The Qur'an tells believers, when they dispute, in Pickthall's words, to "refer it to Allah and the messenger." And a hadith in al-Bukhari says a judge who does his best and gets it right has two rewards, and one who does his best and gets it wrong still has one. Scholars read it as covering any qualified jurist. Disagreement, in Arabic ikhtilaf, is old in Islam. Underneath it, the same Book.

308.title: The heart's polish
308.hook: a well-known saying: everything has a polish, and the heart's polish is remembrance (Bayhaqi)
308.howItsDone: Many Muslims say SubhanAllah, alhamdulillah and Allahu akbar thirty-three or thirty-four times each after prayer or before sleep, often counting on the fingers or on prayer beads, and speak of remembrance as what keeps the heart clear.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ikhtilaf: some love the Sufi orders and shrines, others see them as later additions, and all say keep to the Qur'an. Your line: the same Qur'an underneath.

Before glass mirrors, a mirror was a disc of metal: bronze, silver, polished steel. Leave one in a damp room for a season and it clouds over. Your face in it goes dim, then disappears. Nobody throws the mirror away. You take a cloth, you rub, and your face comes back. A well-known saying, recorded by the scholar al-Bayhaqi and attributed to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ: everything has something that polishes it, and the polish of the heart is the remembrance of Allah. Scholars discuss how strong its chain of narrators is, but the picture has lasted. It closes the Sufi path.
screen: `A METAL MIRROR, CLOUDED OVER.` → `A CLOTH, AND YOUR FACE COMES BACK.` → `THE POLISH OF THE HEART.`

segments.voice: The picture starts in the Qur'an. Speaking of people who have hardened themselves against the truth, it says, in Pickthall's words: "Nay, but that which they have earned is rust upon their hearts." The Arabic word is ran: a film, a tarnish. A hadith in Tirmidhi explains it. When a person does wrong, a dark spot appears on the heart. If they stop, turn back and ask forgiveness, the heart is polished clean. If they keep going, the spot spreads, and that is the ran Allah mentions. So the heart isn't bad. It's a mirror that picks up dust, and the cloth is dhikr, the same work the circles do aloud or in silence. Al-Ghazali, after his crisis, wrote of the heart as a mirror that can show the truth once it's cleaned. Rumi tells a story in the Masnavi: the Chinese and the Greeks hold a painting contest. The Chinese cover their wall with color. The Greeks paint nothing. They polish their wall, and when the curtain between the two is lifted, it shines back everything the Chinese painted, and more. Rumi says the Greeks are like the Sufis, who have polished their hearts. Rabi'a's love, Junayd's sobriety, the reed flute's longing, the circles of gathered remembrance, the nafs being trained: under each is the same slow work with the cloth. And remember yesterday: not every Muslim walks the Sufi orders, but the call to remember Allah comes from the Qur'an itself, and belongs to no single group.
screen: `RUST UPON THEIR HEARTS` · `A MIRROR THAT PICKS UP DUST` · `THE CLOTH IS REMEMBRANCE` · `THE GREEKS POLISHED THEIR WALL`

segments.voice: A pattern from a hadith in al-Bukhari, which the Prophet taught his daughter Fatimah for bedtime: SubhanAllah thirty-three times, alhamdulillah thirty-three, Allahu akbar thirty-four. If you pray, say them softly now, counting on your fingers; if you're learning, say one phrase at a time, each one a single pass of the cloth. Slowly matters more than finishing, and you can finish the hundred afterward.
Dhikr. Remembrance of God — the cloth that, a hadith says, polishes the dust a heart gathers. Today's word.
Your line: polish the heart. Day three hundred eight, and the Sufi path is complete.
